parsed.title: Simulation for Training and Evaluating Driving Policies
outline: Introduction to Simulation and Mid-Level Representations
End-to-End CNN Approach for Autonomous Driving
Comparison of RNN and CNN Methods
parsed.markdown:
Simulation environments and mid-level input representations are used to facilitate autonomous driving training and testing. ChauffeurNet is a recurrent neural network (RNN) that takes mid-level input and outputs driving trajectories for control, enabling training on real or simulated data and closed-loop simulation testing before real deployment [1]. CARLA is an open-source urban driving simulator that supports development, training, and validation of autonomous urban driving systems, including flexible specification of sensor suites and environmental conditions [2]. CARLA provides free urban environment content such as urban layouts, vehicles, buildings, and pedestrians, and supports training, prototyping, and validation of autonomous driving models including perception and control [2]. It also provides measurements of agent state and traffic rule compliance, such as vehicle footprint on wrong-way lanes or sidewalks, traffic light states, and speed limits at vehicle location [2].

ChauffeurNet incorporates components such as FeatureNet and AgentRNN, with recurrent feedback of predictions between iterations, and outputs a heatmap over the next pose, from which a coarse pose prediction is derived [1]. In contrast, an end-to-end convolutional neural network (CNN) approach learns the entire processing pipeline to steer an automobile, generating steering commands from a single front-facing center camera [3]. CARLA is used to study three autonomous driving approaches: classic modular pipeline, end-to-end imitation learning, and end-to-end reinforcement learning [2].

Mid-level input representations enable simulation-based closed-loop testing before real-world deployment, as demonstrated by ChauffeurNet's approach [1]. This contrasts with the end-to-end CNN method, which learns the entire processing pipeline from raw images [3]. CARLA provides a platform that aligns well with mid-level representation approaches for closed-loop testing [2].

There is a contradiction in input and output representations between the end-to-end CNN and ChauffeurNet RNN methods: the CNN generates steering commands directly from camera images, while ChauffeurNet outputs driving trajectories based on mid-level inputs [1,3]. Despite detailed descriptions of these methods, there is a lack of direct comparative evaluation of these two approaches under the same conditions or metrics, limiting understanding of their relative strengths and weaknesses in autonomous driving tasks [1,3].
